transcript.text: panasonic nn h98 not heating anymore, any fix?

There may well be a simple fix, but it depends on what's behind it. If it turns out to be the high-voltage heating side, that isn't a DIY repair. The most likely causes, in order:
1. A setting problem. It could be on a low power level, defrost, or grill/combi mode, or only the clock was set rather than a timed cook started.
2. A fault in the high-voltage heating circuit. Panasonic microwaves are typically inverter models, and on those the inverter board is usually the first suspect, with the magnetron second. Only an engineer can test which one it is.
3. Less often, the door isn't latching fully, so the heating circuit never switches on. One thing to check: if "H98" (or H97) is actually showing on the display rather than being part of the model number, that's Panasonic's code for a fault in the inverter/magnetron heating circuit. Quick checks, all safe:
1. Make sure it's set to normal microwave on full power, not defrost, a low level or grill/combi, and that you start a timed cook. If it heats now, it was just the setting.
2. Heat a cup of water on full power for one minute. Hot means it's working. Still cold means the problem is real.
3. Close the door firmly and listen for a clean click, and wipe any food off the latch area. If it behaves as though the door is open, the door/interlock is the lead rather than the heating parts.
4. Watch what it does while it runs. Does it keep running normally but stay cold, or cut out after a few seconds? A repeatable short cut-out is a strong sign of the inverter/magnetron circuit. If the settings and door are fine and the water stays cold, please don't open the casing. The high-voltage parts can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged, so that needs a microwave engineer. On an older or cheaper microwave, an inverter board or magnetron repair can cost close to a new one, so it's worth getting a quote before deciding. What does it do when you start it?
h98 is what the screen says when it stops; the model on the back is NN-CD87KSBPQ. runs a few seconds in microwave mode then stops. grill heats fine

That clears it up. On Panasonic microwaves, H98 means the microwave power circuit isn't working properly. The control starts the inverter, sees it isn't drawing power as expected, and shuts it down after a few seconds. That matches exactly what yours is doing. The grill working is useful. It shows the mains supply, the control panel and the door switching are all fine, so the fault is in the microwave heating side. 1. The inverter board, which is the usual first suspect on Panasonic inverter models with this code.
2. The magnetron, the second suspect. An engineer can tell the two apart with a test.
3. Less likely, a one-off electronic glitch or a poor supply, which a reset can sometimes clear. 1. Unplug it at the wall for about 5 minutes, then plug it back in. This resets the electronics. If it then heats a cup of water normally for a minute, it was a glitch, but keep an eye on it in case H98 comes back.
2. Plug it straight into a wall socket rather than an extension lead or adaptor. Inverter microwaves draw a lot of power and can trip their own checks on a weak connection. Then try the cup of water again. If it still stops with H98 after a few seconds, that suggests a fault in the high-voltage heating circuit. Please don't open the casing. These parts can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged, so a microwave engineer needs to test whether it's the inverter board or the magnetron. A magnetron replacement costs more, so get a quote and compare it with a new one before going ahead. You can still use the grill in the meantime. How did it get on after the reset and the wall socket?
[Safety panel] Don't remove the microwave's casing or try to repair it inside. Parts inside a microwave can hold a dangerous electric charge even after it's unplugged — have it checked by a qualified engineer.
unplugged it for 5 mins, same thing, h98 again after a few seconds. cup of water still cold. is it worth repairing, it was about £300

On a £300 combi microwave, a repair is often worth it, but it mainly depends on the machine's age and which part has failed. H98 coming straight back after a reset, with the water still cold, suggests a genuine fault in the microwave heating circuit. It isn't a glitch. On Panasonic inverter models the inverter board is the most likely culprit, with the magnetron second. The grill working shows the rest of the machine (control, supply and door) is healthy, which helps the case for repair. How to decide:
1. Check your cover first. If it's within its guarantee, contact Panasonic or the retailer and it should cost you nothing. Even outside that, if it's only a few years old you may have a claim against the retailer under the Consumer Rights Act. A £300 microwave failing early isn't reasonable durability.
2. Get a quote that includes diagnosis. An engineer will test which part it is. As a rough guide, an inverter board repair including labour is usually well under the price of a new combi like yours. A magnetron tends to cost more. A sensible rule is to repair if the quote is under about half the replacement cost and the machine is otherwise in good order.
3. Ask for a fixed price before any work starts, so you can still walk away if it turns out to be the magnetron and the cost climbs. If it's older than about 7 to 8 years, or the quote comes in near half the price of a new one, replacing it is usually the better buy. Either way, please don't open the casing yourself. The high-voltage parts can stay charged even when unplugged. You can keep using the grill meanwhile. Roughly how old is it, and do you still have the receipt or any guarantee paperwork?
[Safety panel] Don't remove the microwave's casing or try to repair it inside. Parts inside a microwave can hold a dangerous electric charge even after it's unplugged — have it checked by a qualified engineer.
about 6 years old. don't know about warranty or receipt. so is it worth getting an engineer out?

Yes, I think it's worth getting an engineer to look at it, as long as you agree a fixed price before any work starts. At six years old a £300 combi is borderline but still worth repairing if it turns out to be the cheaper fault. Why it's worth a look: H98 returning straight after a reset, with the water still cold, points to the microwave heating circuit. On Panasonic inverter models the inverter board is the most likely part, with the magnetron second. Only an engineer's test can tell which. The grill working shows the rest of the machine is healthy, so you're not throwing money at a machine that's failing all over. How to make it pay:
1. Before you book, spend two minutes checking cover. Search your email or bank or card statements for the purchase, which gives you the date and retailer. Also check whether your home insurance or a bank account package includes appliance cover. In England and Wales you can bring a claim against the retailer up to six years after purchase (five in Scotland), so you may be right at the edge. Contact the retailer quickly if it's close.
2. Ask the engineer for a diagnosis plus a fixed quote for each outcome. Then decide.
3. If it's the inverter board, repairing it is usually good value at this age.
4. If it's the magnetron, or the quote comes near half the price of a comparable new combi, replacing it is usually the better buy at six years. If you'd rather not pay a call-out fee on a six-year-old machine at all, replacing it is a reasonable choice too. Just don't open it up yourself, because the high-voltage parts can stay charged even when unplugged. The grill is fine to use in the meantime.
[Safety panel] Don't remove the microwave's casing or try to repair it inside. Parts inside a microwave can hold a dangerous electric charge even after it's unplugged — have it checked by a qualified engineer.
